claim: Experience-based plasticity of the human cortex mediates the influence of individual experience on cognition and behavior.
source: Experience-based plasticity of the human cortex mediates the influence of individual experience on cognition and behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about brain plasticity presented in the abstract and introduction without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: The complete loss of a sensory modality is among the most extreme experiences affecting the human cortex.
source: The complete loss of a sensory modality is among the most extreme such experiences.
evidence: This is a characterization of sensory loss based on established understanding in the field.

claim: Sensory braille letter representations are located in tactile processing areas (S1, S2, aIPS, and pIPS).
source: We found the difference to be significant in tactile processing areas (S1, S2, aIPS, and pIPS) and in LOC, but not elsewhere (Figure 2B, middle).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI ROI analysis showing significant differences between within-hand and across-hand classification in these regions.

claim: Perceptual braille letter representations are located in sighted reading areas (EVC, LOC, and VWFA).
source: We found significant information (Figure 2B, right) only in sighted reading areas (EVC, LOC, and VWFA), with the exception of the insula.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI ROI analysis showing significant across-hand classification in these regions.

claim: LOC serves as a 'hinge' region containing both sensory and perceptual braille letter representations.
source: Notably, LOC is the only region that contained both sensory and perceptual braille letter representations. This suggests a 'hinge' function in the transformation from sensory to perceptual braille letter representations.
evidence: This claim is based on the finding that LOC showed significant results in both sensory and perceptual analyses.

claim: Sensory braille letter representations emerge at 77 ms after stimulus onset.
source: This difference became significant at 77 ms (45–138 ms) (Figure 3A, black curve).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-resolved EEG classification analysis showing the onset of significant differences between within-hand and across-hand classification.

claim: Perceptual braille letter representations emerge at 184 ms after stimulus onset.
source: In contrast, the across-hand classification, indicating perceptual representations, became significant later at 184 ms (127–230 ms) (Figure 3A, green curve).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-resolved EEG classification analysis showing the onset of significant across-hand classification.

claim: Sensory braille letter representations emerge before perceptual braille letter representations.
source: Compared to sensory representations, the significance onset of perceptual representations was delayed by 107 ms (21–167 ms) (N = 11, 1000 bootstraps, one-tailed bootstrap test against zero, p = 0.012).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of onset latencies from EEG data.

claim: Perceptual representations in EVC, LOC, VWFA, and insula are significantly correlated with behavioral similarity ratings.
source: Considering braille letter representations in space through fMRI (Figure 4B, N = 15, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05, FDR corrected), we found that previously identified perceptual representations (i.e., identified by the across-hand analysis) in EVC, LOC, VWFA, and insula showed significant correlations with behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis correlating fMRI RDMs with behavioral RDMs.

claim: Sensory representations in S1, S2, aIPS, pIPS, and LOC are not significantly correlated with behavioral similarity ratings.
source: In contrast, sensory representations (i.e., identified by the differences between within- and across-hand analyses) in S1, S2, aIPS, pIPS, and LOC were not significantly correlated with behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by representational similarity analysis showing no significant correlations for sensory representations in these regions.

claim: Cortical structures most strongly activated by visual input in sighted brains are activated by other cognitive functions in visually deprived brains.
source: Previous research has shown that cortical structures most strongly activated by visual input in sighted brains are activated by a plethora of other cognitive functions in visually deprived brains (Bedny, 2017), including braille reading (Büchel et al., 1998; Burton et al., 2012; Rączy et al., 2019; Reich et al., 2011; Sadato et al., 1998; Uhl et al., 1991; Sadato, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in the field.

claim: Braille readers commonly use both hands, requiring their brain to transform sensory tactile input into a hand-independent perceptual format.
source: Braille readers commonly use both hands, requiring their brain to transform sensory tactile input into a hand-independent perceptual format.
evidence: This is a statement about braille reading practice based on general knowledge of braille reading.

claim: Within-hand classification of braille letters was significantly above chance in regions associated with both tactile processing (S1, S2, aIPS, pIPS, and insula) and sighted reading (EVC, LOC, LFA, and VWFA).
source: We found that within-hand classification of braille letters was significantly above chance in regions associated with both tactile processing (S1, S2, anterior intra-parietal sulcus [aIPS], posterior intra-parietal sulcus [pIPS], and insula) and sighted reading (EVC, LOC, LFA, and VWFA) (Figure 2B, left; N = 15, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05, false discovery rate [FDR] corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI ROI classification analysis with statistical testing.

claim: EVC in the visually deprived brain harbors representations of single braille letters at a higher perceptual level rather than a tactile input level.
source: More specifically, our finding that EVC represents perceptual rather than sensory braille letter information indicates that EVC representations are formatted at a higher perceptual level rather than a tactile input level.
evidence: This claim is based on the finding that EVC showed significant perceptual but not sensory representations, combined with inference about the nature of these representations.

claim: EVC in blind participants processes natural sounds.
source: Previous studies also found that EVC of blind participants processes other higher-level information such as natural sounds (Vetter et al., 2020; Mattioni et al., 2020) and language (Burton et al., 2002; Burton et al., 2003b; Röder et al., 2002; Bedny et al., 2011; Lane et al., 2015; Dietrich et al., 2013; Watkins et al., 2022; Abboud et al., 2019; Amedi et al., 2003; Burton, 2003a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: EVC in blind participants processes language.
source: Previous studies also found that EVC of blind participants processes other higher-level information such as natural sounds (Vetter et al., 2020; Mattioni et al., 2020) and language (Burton et al., 2002; Burton et al., 2003b; Röder et al., 2002; Bedny et al., 2011; Lane et al., 2015; Dietrich et al., 2013; Watkins et al., 2022; Abboud et al., 2019; Amedi et al., 2003; Burton, 2003a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: VWFA contains perceptual but not sensory braille letter representations.
source: We found that VWFA contains perceptual but not sensory braille letter representations.
evidence: This claim is based on the fMRI ROI analysis results showing significant perceptual but not sensory representations in VWFA.

claim: The functional organization of the VWFA is modality-independent.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the functional organization of the VWFA is modality-independent (Reich et al., 2011) depicting an important contribution to the ongoing debate on how visual experience shapes representations along the ventral stream (Bedny, 2021).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current findings combined with citation to previous work.

claim: Shape serves as an intermediate level representational format in LOC between lower-level tactile properties and higher-level perceptual letter features.
source: We stipulate that shape serves as an intermediate level representational format in between lower-level properties such as specific location of tactile stimulation or dot number in braille letters and higher-level perceptual letter features (Amedi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the LOC findings, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The somatosensory cortices and intra-parietal sulci represent hand-dependent but not hand-independent braille letter representations.
source: We observed that the somatosensory cortices and intra-parietal sulci represent hand-dependent but not hand-independent braille letter representations.
evidence: This claim is based on the fMRI ROI analysis results showing significant sensory but not perceptual representations in these regions.

claim: Primary somatosensory cortex represents the location of tactile stimulation.
source: This is consistent with previous studies reporting that the primary somatosensory cortex represents the location of tactile stimulation (Sanchez-Panchuelo et al., 2012), but not the identity of braille words (Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Primary somatosensory cortex does not represent the identity of braille words.
source: This is consistent with previous studies reporting that the primary somatosensory cortex represents the location of tactile stimulation (Sanchez-Panchuelo et al., 2012), but not the identity of braille words (Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The insula plays a role in tactile memory in the sighted brain.
source: Based on previous studies in the sighted brain, the insula plays a role in tactile memory (Bonda et al., 1996; Burton and Sinclair, 2000; Reed et al., 2004) and multisensory integration (Banati et al., 2000; Hadjikhani and Roland, 1998; Prather et al., 2004; Naghavi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The insula plays a role in multisensory integration in the sighted brain.
source: Based on previous studies in the sighted brain, the insula plays a role in tactile memory (Bonda et al., 1996; Burton and Sinclair, 2000; Reed et al., 2004) and multisensory integration (Banati et al., 2000; Hadjikhani and Roland, 1998; Prather et al., 2004; Naghavi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sequential multi-step processing in time is a general principle of information processing in the human brain.
source: Such sequential multi-step processing in time is a general principle of information processing in the human brain, also known in the visual (Isik et al., 2014; Carlson et al., 2013; Cichy et al., 2014) and auditory (Lowe et al., 2021) domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in visual and auditory domains.

claim: Braille letter classification peaks substantially later in time (~200 ms for hand-dependent and ~390 ms for hand-independent representations) than visually presented words, letters, objects, and object categories (~125 ms for location-dependent and ~175 ms for location-independent representations).
source: Our results indicate that braille letter classification peaks substantially later in time (~200 ms for hand-dependent and ~390 ms for hand-independent representations) than previously reported classification of visually presented words, letters, objects, and object categories (e.g., ~125 ms for location-dependent and ~175 ms for location-independent representations) (Isik et al., 2014; Carlson et al., 2013; Cichy et al., 2014; Ling et al., 2019; Teng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim compares the current EEG findings with previous research on visual processing.

claim: Tactile information reaches the cortex as early as 35 ms after stimulation onset.
source: We find that tactile information reaches the cortex fast: we can classify which hand was stimulated as early as 35 ms after stimulation onset (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG classification analysis of hand identity.

claim: Braille reading is slower than print reading.
source: Braille reading is slower than print reading (Bola et al., 2016; Brysbaert, 2019) even if participants are fluent braille readers.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Blind participants have higher listening rates than sighted participants.
source: Blind participants have higher listening rates (Bragg et al., 2018) and better auditory discrimination skills (Hötting and Röder, 2009) than sighted participants, indicating more efficient auditory processing (Röder et al., 1996; Muchnik et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Blind participants have better auditory discrimination skills than sighted participants.
source: Blind participants have higher listening rates (Bragg et al., 2018) and better auditory discrimination skills (Hötting and Röder, 2009) than sighted participants, indicating more efficient auditory processing (Röder et al., 1996; Muchnik et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The temporal dynamics with which braille letter representations emerge are limited by the particular efficiency of the braille letter system, rather than the capacity of the brain.
source: Together, this result pattern suggests that the temporal dynamics with which braille letter representations emerge are limited by the particular efficiency of the braille letter system, rather than the capacity of the brain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing braille reading speed with auditory processing efficiency in blind participants.

claim: The similarity between perceptual braille letter representations and behavioral similarity ratings emerges in a time window in which transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the VWFA affects braille letter reading in sighted braille readers.
source: Interestingly, the similarity between perceptual braille letter representations and behavioral similarity ratings emerges in a time window in which transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the VWFA affects braille letter reading in sighted braille readers (Bola et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim relates the current RSA findings to previous TMS research.

claim: Around 320–420 ms after the onset of reading braille, visually deprived and sighted brains utilize braille letter representations for performing tasks such as letter identification.
source: This implies that around 320–420 ms after the onset of reading braille, visually deprived and sighted brains utilize braille letter representations for performing tasks such as letter identification.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing of RSA results and comparison with TMS findings.

claim: Fifteen participants completed the fMRI experiment.
source: Sixteen participants completed the fMRI experiment. One person was excluded due to technical problems during the recording, leaving a total of 15 participants in the fMRI experiment (mean age 39 years, SD = 10, 9 females).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the participant sample in the methods section.

claim: Eleven participants participated in the EEG experiment.
source: Eleven participants participated in the EEG experiment (N = 11, mean age 44 years, SD = 10, 8 females).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the participant sample in the methods section.

claim: All participants were blind since birth or early childhood (≤3 years).
source: All participants were blind since birth or early childhood (≤3 years, for details see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant characteristics in the methods section.

claim: Eight braille letters (B, C, D, L, M, N, V, and Z) entered the main analysis.
source: Eight letters entered the main analysis. Two letters (E and O) served as vigilance targets to which participants responded with their foot; these trials were excluded from all analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design in the results section.

claim: Braille stimuli were presented using single piezo-electric refreshable cells.
source: We delivered the braille stimuli using single piezo-electric refreshable cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental apparatus in the results section.

claim: The experimental setup allowed participants to read braille letters without moving their finger, thus avoiding finger motion artifacts.
source: This allowed participants to read braille letters without moving their finger, thus avoiding finger motion artifacts in the brain signal and analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: In fMRI, trials consisted of a 500-ms stimulus presentation followed by an inter-stimulus interval (ISI) of 2500 ms.
source: The stimuli were presented in random order, with each trial consisting of a 500-ms stimulus presentation to either the right or left hand. In fMRI, all trials were followed by an inter-stimulus interval (ISI) of 2500 ms to account for the sluggishness of the BOLD response (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental timing in the results section.

claim: In EEG, standard trials had an ISI of 500 ms while catch trials had an ISI of 1100 ms.
source: In EEG, standard trials had an ISI of 500 ms while catch trials had an ISI of 1100 ms in order to avoid movement contaminations.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental timing in the results section.

claim: The average performance for braille letter identification with the left hand was 89% correct (SD = 10).
source: The average performance for the left hand was 89% correct (SD = 10) and for the right hand it was 88% correct (SD = 13).
evidence: This is a direct statement about behavioral performance in the screening task.

claim: The average performance for braille letter identification with the right hand was 88% correct (SD = 13).
source: The average performance for the left hand was 89% correct (SD = 10) and for the right hand it was 88% correct (SD = 13).
evidence: This is a direct statement about behavioral performance in the screening task.

claim: Perceptual representations in sighted reading areas are suitably formatted to guide behavior.
source: This indicates that perceptual braille letter representations in sighted reading areas are suitably formatted to guide behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RSA results showing significant correlations between perceptual representations and behavior.

claim: Both earlier sensory representations and later perceptual representations of braille letters are suitably formatted to guide behavior.
source: This indicates that both earlier sensory representations and later perceptual representations of braille letters are suitable formatted to guide behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EEG RSA results showing significant correlations for both sensory and perceptual representations with behavior.

claim: The onset latency difference between sensory and perceptual representations in the EEG-behavior RSA was 240 ms (−81 to 636 ms) and was significant (p = 0.046).
source: The onset latency differences of 240 ms (−81 to 636 ms) (N = 11, 1000 bootstrap, one-tailed bootstrap test against zero, p = 0.046) was significant.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from the EEG RSA analysis.

claim: EVC in the visually deprived brain might not be undergoing fundamental changes in brain organization.
source: Thus, EVC in the visually deprived brain might not be undergoing fundamental changes in brain organization (Seydell-Greenwald et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: EVC in general has the capacity to process higher-level information.
source: This suggests that EVC, in general, has the capacity to process higher-level information (Pascual-Leone and Hamilton, 2001).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current findings and previous research, supported by citation.

claim: Natural sound representations are located in EVC of sighted participants.
source: Natural sound representations (Vetter et al., 2020) and language activations (Seydell-Greenwald et al., 2023) are also located in EVC of sighted participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Language activations are located in EVC of sighted participants.
source: Natural sound representations (Vetter et al., 2020) and language activations (Seydell-Greenwald et al., 2023) are also located in EVC of sighted participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The cortex is capable of dynamic adjustments within pre-existing computational capacity limits.
source: This promotes a view of brain plasticity in which the cortex is capable of dynamic adjustments within pre-existing computational capacity limits (Bedny, 2017; Seydell-Greenwald et al., 2023; Pascual-Leone and Hamilton, 2001; Makin and Krakauer, 2023).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The functional organization of both VWFA and LOC is multimodal.
source: Fourth, the finding of letter representations of tactile origin in both VWFA and LOC indicate that the functional organization of both regions is multimodal, contributing to the debate on how experience from vision or other sensory modalities shapes representations along the ventral stream (Bedny, 2021; Amedi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current findings that VWFA and LOC represent tactile braille information.

claim: Tactile processing areas represent sensory rather than higher-level features of tactile inputs in visually deprived brains.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that these tactile processing areas represent sensory rather than higher-level features of tactile inputs in visually deprived brains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings combined with previous research.

claim: Early thalamic connections exist to both S1 and V1 in visually deprived brains.
source: First, the coexistence of early thalamic connections to both S1 and V1 (Müller et al., 2019) would enable EVC to receive from different sources and at different time points.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on connectivity.

claim: Potentially overlapping connections from both sensory cortices to other visual or parietal areas exist in visually deprived brains.
source: Second, potentially overlapping connections from both sensory cortices to other visual or parietal areas (Ioannides et al., 2013) could enable the visually deprived brain to process information in a widespread and interconnected array of brain areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on connectivity.

claim: In the visually deprived brain, several brain areas receive and forward information at the same time in a spatially and functionally distributed and overlapping fashion.
source: In such a network architecture, several brain areas receive and forward information at the same time. In contrast to information discretely traveling from one processing unit to the next in the sighted brain's processing cascade, we can rather picture information flowing in a spatially and functionally more distributed and overlapping fashion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how information flow might be organized in the visually deprived brain.

claim: The human brain, even in extreme instances of species-atypical cortical plasticity, honors the principle of sequential multi-step processing in time.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the human brain, even in extreme instances of species-atypical cortical plasticity, honors this principle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current EEG findings showing sequential emergence of sensory and perceptual representations.

claim: Regions typically processing visual information adapt to represent perceptual braille letter information in the visually deprived brain.
source: On the one hand, our findings emphasize how plastic the brain is by showing that regions typically processing visual information adapt to represent perceptual braille letter information.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the fMRI findings showing perceptual representations in sighted reading areas.

claim: Brain areas represent information from atypical inputs within the boundaries of their pre-existing computational capacity.
source: Brain areas represent information from atypical inputs within the boundaries of their pre-existing computational capacity and the progression from sensory to perceptual transformations adheres to a common temporal scheme and functional role.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the findings about the limits of plasticity.

claim: The progression from sensory to perceptual transformations adheres to a common temporal scheme and functional role.
source: Brain areas represent information from atypical inputs within the boundaries of their pre-existing computational capacity and the progression from sensory to perceptual transformations adheres to a common temporal scheme and functional role.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the EEG findings showing sequential processing.

claim: Overlapping functional responses alone cannot inform us about the nature of the observed activations.
source: However, overlapping functional responses alone cannot inform us about the nature of the observed activations, that is, what kind of information they represent and thus what role they play in cognitive processing.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research approaches, based on general knowledge of neuroimaging methods.

claim: Sensory braille letter representations are operationalized as representations coding information specific to the hand that was reading (hand-dependent).
source: We operationalize sensory braille letter representations as representations coding information specific to the hand that was reading (hand-dependent).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the operational definition used in the study.

claim: Perceptual braille letter representations are operationalized as representations coding information independent of which hand was reading (hand-independent).
source: In contrast, we operationalize perceptual braille letter representations as representations coding information independent of which hand was reading (hand-independent).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the operational definition used in the study.

claim: Braille letter representations are located in the assessed ROIs without revealing any additional regions beyond the hypothesized ROIs.
source: The results confirmed that braille letter representations are located in the assessed ROIs without revealing any additional regions (Figure 2C, N = 15, height threshold p < 0.001, cluster-level family-wise error [FWE] corrected p < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI searchlight analysis results.

claim: Within-hand classification became significant at 62 ms (29–111 ms).
source: We found that within-hand classification became significant at 62 ms (29–111 ms) (Figure 3A, blue curve).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the EEG classification onset latency results.

claim: In the time window of highest decodability (~200–300 ms), sensory braille letter information was decodable from widespread electrodes across the scalp.
source: In the time window of highest decodability (~200–300 ms), sensory braille letter information was decodable from widespread electrodes across the scalp.
evidence: This claim is based on the EEG searchlight analysis in sensor space.

claim: Perceptual braille letter information was decodable later and from overall fewer electrodes which were located over right frontal, central, left parietal, and left temporal areas.
source: In contrast, perceptual braille letter information was decodable later and from overall fewer electrodes which were located over right frontal, central, left parietal, and left temporal areas (Figure 3B; N = 11, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05, FDR corrected across electrodes and time points).
evidence: This claim is based on the EEG searchlight analysis in sensor space.

claim: Sensory braille letter information is represented in more widespread brain areas than perceptual braille letter information.
source: These additional results reinforce that sensory braille letter information is represented in more widespread brain areas than perceptual braille letter information, corroborating our ROI classification results.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EEG searchlight results.

claim: Not all representations that distinguish between braille letters have to be used by the brain to guide behavior; some might be epiphenomenal.
source: However, not all of these representations have to be used by the brain to guide behavior; some of these representations might be epiphenomenal and only available to the experimenter (deWit et al., 2016; Reddy and Kanwisher, 2007; Williams et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of neural representations, supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: If two stimuli are perceived to be similar, they will also elicit similar actions.
source: The idea is that if two stimuli are perceived to be similar, they will also elicit similar actions (Cichy et al., 2019; Bankson et al., 2018; Mur et al., 2013; Charest et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for using perceived similarity as a proxy for behavioral relevance, supported by citations.

claim: Nineteen participants completed the behavioral letter similarity rating task.
source: Out of a total of 21 participants, 19 participants (excluding one fMRI and one EEG participant) completed an additional behavioral task in which they rated the perceived similarity of braille letter pairs.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the participant sample in the behavioral experiment.

claim: The onset of significant correlations between sensory representations and behavior in EEG occurred at 220 ms (167–567 ms).
source: The temporal dynamics mirrored those of the EEG classification analysis (Figure 3A), in that the results related to sensory representations emerged earlier at 220 ms (167–567 ms) than the results related to perceptual representations at 466 ms (249–877 ms).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the EEG RSA onset latency results.

claim: The onset of significant correlations between perceptual representations and behavior in EEG occurred at 466 ms (249–877 ms).
source: The temporal dynamics mirrored those of the EEG classification analysis (Figure 3A), in that the results related to sensory representations emerged earlier at 220 ms (167–567 ms) than the results related to perceptual representations at 466 ms (249–877 ms).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the EEG RSA onset latency results.

claim: Previous research has identified the regions activated during braille reading in high detail.
source: Previous research has identified the regions activated during braille reading in high detail (Büchel et al., 1998; Burton et al., 2012; Rączy et al., 2019; Reich et al., 2011; Sadato et al., 1998; Uhl et al., 1991; Sadato, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Activation in a brain region alone does not indicate its functional role or the kind of information it represents.
source: However, activation in a brain region alone does not indicate its functional role or the kind of information it represents (Haynes and Rees, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of activation-based analyses, supported by citation.

claim: VWFA is functionally selective for letter and word stimuli in the visually deprived brain.
source: By clarifying the representational format of language representations in VWFA, our results support previous findings of the VWFA being functionally selective for letter and word stimuli in the visually deprived brain (Reich et al., 2011; Striem-Amit et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is based on the current findings combined with citations to previous research.
